title: Onprem airgapped runtime performance & offline licensing deep dive
summary: Deep technical session covering on-prem artifact delivery, offline GPU driver licensing, runtime performance (latency/throughput), KV cache behavior, batching strategies, and quantization tradeoffs for an air-gapped deployment. Action items include offline driver package workflow, secure artifact transfer checklist, and follow up benchmark run with 8k context model.
topics: batching strategies and autoscaling in private envs

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-02
Start time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~85 minutes
Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marco (Redwood SE), Lena (Orion Head of Platform), Tom (Infra), Sofia (Security), Ben (ML)
---
00:00 Jared: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you making time, this is the deep dive we scoped around on premise airgap, artifact delivery, and the driver/license flow. we'll try to cover perf numbers, caching, batching and then leave time for the offline licensing questions.
00:35 Lena: thanks jared. wanted to make sure security is on the line because the way we run air-gapped installs is pretty strict. sofia is here.
00:52 Sofia: hi all, i'll mostly be listening but will jump in on compliance and encryption stuff.
01:10 Priya: great, i'll start with a quick overview of how our private deployment artifacts are delivered in an air-gapped scenario, then run through runtime considerations. note: some product names may get munged in transcription, sorry in advance.
01:35 Marco: first slide, artifact bundles — we provide a signed tarball containing the runtime, model artifacts (packaged weights), runtime libs, and a driver compatibility matrix. for air-gapped customers we produce an offline artifacts bundle plus a checksum and an RSA signature.
01:55 Tom: how large are we talking for a typical LLM package? our infra folks need to plan transfer windows.
02:05 Marco: for a 70B model quantized to 4-bit and necessary runtime libs it's normally in the 25-45GB range. if you include multiple model variants or extra quant packs you could see 60-120GB. we recommend staging via physical media for initial sync.
02:30 Ben: do you support incremental patch bundles so we don't reseed the whole image every time?
02:40 Priya: yes — we have delta bundles for model weight patches and runtime patches, and a deterministic patch manifest so you can apply only changed shards. that reduces transfer size substantially.
03:05 Jared: on the licensing side — offline GPU driver licensing, what we call "driver tokens" — how does that look? marco take it.
03:18 Marco: offline licensing is two-step. we generate a license request file with hardware fingerprints (or a hardware config file you supply), you sign it and send via approved channel, we return a signed license blob. for fully air-gapped sites we can also provide a time-limited license that you install with the bundle. documentation includes HSM/KMS integration notes.
03:45 Sofia: are there audits on the license exchange? we need a paper trail for auditors.
03:52 Marco: yes we provide a signed manifest and chain of custody PDF, and can push a signed S3/object manifest if you use a transfer partner. offline transfer notes include how to verify signatures and checksums.
04:20 Tom: question on GPU driver compatibility — do you package NVIDIA drivers? some of our clusters are older A100 gen1 and some are H100.
04:35 Priya: we don't distribute NVIDIA proprietary drivers directly, due to licensing; instead we provide a driver adapter and an offline driver installer wrapper script plus a vendor-specific driver package list and exact version you must fetch from the GPU vendor. for some customers we facilitate procurement of offline driver bundles under their own enterprise agreements, but Redwood doesn't re-distribute vendor binary blobs unless contractually allowed.
05:05 Lena: so the customer is responsible for fetching NVIDIA blobs, and Redwood helps validate and wrap them?
05:12 Marco: exactly. we validate checksums and provide wrapper scripts to install in the expected runtime paths, and we include a compatibility shim for kernel module path differences.
05:30 Ben: for the runtime performance stuff — priya, can you talk about latency/throughput tradeoffs and how kv cache and batching play into it?
05:38 Priya: sure. at a high level we optimize the serving runtime for two modes: low latency single-request flows and high throughput batched flows. critical levers are batch size, sequence length cap, KV caching configuration (prefix caching vs full session), and quantization profile.
06:05 Priya: example: for a 70B model at 2k context, single-request latencies on an H100 with optimized kernels can be 120-180ms per token depending on prompt complexity and decoding settings; in batched mode with 8 concurrent streams and N=8 batching you might drop to 25-40ms per token effective cost but with increased tail latency for first token.
06:40 Tom: those are useful numbers. our SLO is 200ms for chat front-end, so single-request mode is important. can you preserve that under load?
06:52 Priya: yes — recommend dedicated capacity with pinned GPU pools for predictable tail latency. also configure continuous batching thresholds: max batch delay 10ms, but route premium traffic to reserved nodes.
07:15 Jared: should we talk briefly about KV cache? customers often want to store conversation state to avoid recomputing prefixes.
07:25 Priya: KV cache is best used for prefix caching across sessions where prefix tokens are stable — e.g., system prompt, user profile. with our runtime you can persist and restore KV shards per session. in air-gapped setups we provide a local secure key-value store overlay and optional encrypted KV dump export/import for migration.
07:55 Ben: is the KV store in-memory only or backed to disk? recovery semantics?
08:05 Marco: by default it's in-memory for speed with periodic checkpointing to local encrypted files. checkpoint interval is configurable; we support fast restart with snapshot restore to avoid cold-cache decoding cost.
08:25 Sofia: encryption of checkpoint files? we need AES-GCM and key wrap with KMS/HSM.
08:32 Priya: yes, checkpoint files are AES-GCM encrypted and keys are wrapped by your KMS/HSM. for fully air-gapped sites we can accept key material provisioned via a hardware token.
08:55 Tom: what about batching strategies — adaptive batching vs fixed? any recommendations for on-prem?
09:05 Priya: adaptive batching that looks at request arrival patterns works well for variable traffic, but it must be tuned to your latency SLO. in practice we run a hybrid: a small fixed core batch for premium routes and adaptive pools for best-effort routes. we expose knobs for max batch size, max latency, and per-route priority.
09:35 Ben: quantization — what quant levels do you support and how does it affect throughput/quality?
09:45 Priya: we support 8-bit, 4-bit (various QAT/QQ formats), and experimental 3-bit in some models. 4-bit (LLM.int4 style) gives ~2.2-3x speedup and ~40-60% memory reduction with minimal quality drop for many tasks, but for sensitive generation you should evaluate with your eval set.
10:15 Marco: we also have hybrid kernels that use 8-bit for attention and 4-bit for FFN to balance accuracy and perf. we'll share quant profiles per model.
10:30 Lena: can you show a quick perf slide or run a small benchmark?
10:36 Marco: sure — i'll run a quick micro-benchmark we often use. (background noise: typing)
11:10 Marco: running an 8-stream batched run on H100 w/ 4-bit profile: throughput ~ 14 tokens/sec per GPU effective, latency first-token ~ 150ms in single-stream; with 8 concurrent streams batching effective per-token internal latency 30ms. numbers are approximate — we'll share raw logs.
11:45 Tom: request: can you produce a benchmark harness we can run internally in our air-gapped environment? we can't call outbound endpoints.
11:55 Marco: yes we have an offline benchmark harness delivered in the artifact bundle. it runs end-to-end with a local loader and can output CSVs. i'll attach config templates.
12:10 Priya: note — for large sequence lengths (8k/16k), memory management and KV eviction policies become critical. we can do chunked attention and recompute strategies; but please expect throughput to drop vs 2k contexts.
12:40 Ben: do you support offloading to host memory for very long contexts?
12:45 Priya: yes — host offload and NVMe spill support exists, with significant latency penalty but it enables very long contexts without OOM. we can tune the windowing and prefetch heuristics.
13:10 Sofia: on the security side, would you be able to provide an attestation of the runtime binary? we need checksums and ideally reproducible builds.
13:20 Marco: we provide signed artifacts and a build manifest. reproducible builds are on our roadmap, we do deterministic builds in many cases but full reproducibility across customer kernels can be tricky.
13:45 Lena: let's talk about the offline driver install workflow end-to-end so our ops team can map it.
13:55 Marco: step 1: customer exports hardware inventory and signs a hardware config file. step 2: Redwood validates and creates an offline license request and returns a signed license blob. step 3: customer obtains vendor driver blobs (e.g., NVIDIA) under their own procurement, we validate checksums and issue an install wrapper. step 4: operations run the provided install script which places drivers in /opt/redwood/drivers and updates module paths, then they run a post-install validation tool that we provide.
14:40 Tom: what about kernel versions? our nodes run a variety of kernels.
14:48 Priya: our shim supports common kernel ABI mismatches, but kernel-specific driver builds are still the customer responsibility. the install wrapper can accept path overrides. for edge cases we offer a hybrid support engagement.
15:10 Lena: any caveats about offline license rotation? if we have long running clusters do we need periodic check-ins?
15:20 Marco: licenses can be time-limited; for longer term we support renewable license blobs that you can re-peek via a renewal token. in fully air-gapped, renewal requires a new signed request; we can support 1-3 year time windows based on contract.
15:45 Sofia: auditors will want logs for license application, can you keep a local audit trail?
15:50 Marco: yes — the agent writes tamper-evident audit logs and we can provide integration guidance to ship those to your SIEM on periodic physical transfer. logs are signed.
16:20 Ben: a practical question — when you say delta bundles for model weights, how do you handle shard alignment and format compat?
16:30 Priya: our delta manifest maps by shard id and byte offset; the patcher applies binary diffs to shard files. we support both sharded and flat weight formats; the bundle includes a compatibility shim to convert if needed.
16:55 Tom: can we see sample checksum artifacts? we need to automate verification.
17:03 Marco: yes, we'll include SHA256 manifests and a small verifier script.
17:25 Jared: let's circle back to performance tuning knobs clients typically change after first pilot.
17:33 Priya: common tweaks: reduce max seq length for NLU routes, enable prefix caching for system prompts, raise batch size for offline batch jobs, use 4-bit quant for internal tooling, pin dedicated GPUs for latency sensitive routes, and increase checkpoint frequency for critical sessions.
18:05 Ben: what about autoscaling in an on-prem context? anything Redwood provides?
18:12 Marco: we provide an orchestrator that can scale via node pools — policy can be time-of-day, queue-depth, or custom metrics. in air-gapped sites autoscaling often maps to powering additional reserved nodes; we handle cluster lifecycle via our private control plane or a local controller depending on the deployment model.
18:45 Tom: will there be extra telemetry leaving the site? we cannot allow outbound telemetry without approval.
18:52 Jared: good call. in private deployments telemetry is opt-in; we have an offline telemetry export feature where logs are packaged and signed for periodic transfer. real-time telemetry must be explicitly enabled and can be routed through customer proxies.
19:20 Sofia: any PII concerns in logs? we need redaction guidance.
19:26 Priya: logs avoid raw prompt content by default unless you opt into full trace; we recommend token-level anonymization and provide a redaction plugin you can run before export.
19:55 Lena: ok this is helpful. can we talk next about rollback/upgrade paths for runtime in locked environments?
20:05 Marco: runtime upgrades are done via staged bundles: canary node set, smoke tests (we provide local api tests), then full rollout. rollback is the inverse — restore previous runtime snapshot and model weights. we include db migration scripts for config only.
20:30 Ben: let's capture the concrete deliverables.
20:35 Jared: action items we captured earlier — priya runbook, marco benchmark harness, lena to share vendor list. we'll also send the offline licensing doc and a sample driver wrapper.
20:50 Marco: one more note on quantization evaluation: we'll run your eval set against 4-bit and 8-bit profiles and deliver a small report with perplexity and task-specific metrics. we recommend starting with 4-bit hybrid kernels.
21:10 Tom: timeline check — we want to start pilot mid-December if docs and artifacts are ready. is that feasible?
21:18 Jared: yes — proposed pilot kickoff week of 2025-12-15, remediation iterations through January, then scale test late Jan.
21:35 Sofia: security will need to review the signed manifest process and the audit logs; we'll send the list of questions.
21:42 Priya: noted, we'll add the compliance checklist to the doc set.
22:00 Lena: thanks everyone — can you email the bundle contents list and the benchmark harness?
22:06 Marco: will do, attaching the harness and sample CSVs in the artifact bundle.
22:18 Jared: great. any last minute questions?
22:25 Ben: one — in the offline driver wrapper, do you support FIPS kernels?
22:30 Marco: we have limited FIPS support, need to validate per-kernel; we'll log as an action to confirm exact kernel compatibility for your nodes.
22:45 Jared: ok we'll log that. thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule.
22:55 Meeting end.
